name: Art deco
basis: why: brightness sets each line's thickness, 'exactly how an engraver works'; hist: thick-and-thin lines from banknote engraving
note: Art deco itself is a style; filed under engraving because the rendering is engraved line weight with a metallic fill. Frame and sunburst are style.

lumenary.blurb: Engraved metallic linework inside a stepped, fan-cornered frame.

facts.from: Paris, then New York and Bombay
facts.bestOn: Portraits and buildings with clear light and dark shapes

why: Art deco loved machines, speed and rich materials, so it drew with metal: strict symmetry, stepped outlines and lines that swell and thin like those on a banknote. Here brightness sets the thickness of each gold line, so the light parts of your picture become fat, gleaming metal and the dark parts shrink to hairlines. The picture is carried by line weight alone, which is exactly how an engraver works.
how: Cover the page with fine horizontal bands, or with rays fanning out from a point below the picture in Sunburst mode.
Measure how bright the picture is along each band or ray.
Make the line thicker where it is bright and thinner where it is dark.
Fill every line with one metallic gradient laid across the whole page, so it reads as polished gold, silver or copper.
Add the stepped double frame, the corner fans and the title.
history: The style takes its name from the 1925 Exposition internationale des arts décoratifs et industriels modernes in Paris. In the 1920s and 30s it spread through posters, cinemas, ocean liners and skyscrapers, and its stepped silhouettes and sunbursts still mark cities from New York to Mumbai. The thick and thin engraved lines used for the metal come from banknote and certificate printing, where fine line work was prized because it was hard to copy.
uses: Invitations, cocktail menus and cinema style posters
Hotel and restaurant branding with a period feel
Themed party graphics and film title cards
terms: A way of printing in which the picture is cut into metal as lines. Thicker lines carry more ink or, here, more metal.
Rays fanning from a single point, a favourite deco motif for rising suns and radio waves.
A border whose corners climb in steps, like the silhouette of a ziggurat or a skyscraper.
paragraphs: Art deco’s signature is geometric ornament in metal. Two engraving techniques are available, both of which turn brightness into the thickness of a gold line rather than into tone. In “Lines” mode the picture is covered with horizontal bands; at every position along a band the band’s thickness is set by the brightness there, so bright areas get fat lines and dark areas hairlines, the technique of banknote engraving. The band is built as a polygon: along the top edge going right, then back along the bottom edge going left.

“Sunburst” does the same with rays fanning from a point below the picture. A ray is a direction; stepping along it samples brightness, and the ray’s width at distance r is capped at its angular share of the circle (so neighbouring rays never overlap) and shrunk by brightness. The metal is a five-stop gradient laid diagonally across the whole picture, which is what makes it read as polished gold, silver or copper. Frame ornament (double border, corner fans of three arcs and radial ticks, midpoint diamonds) is drawn with arcs and short lines, and the title is set in Bodoni with extra letter-spacing.

equations.note: Thickness of a line band at x; y_c is the band’s centre line.
Ray width at distance r from the origin: never wider than its slice Δα·r.

presets.text: Switch to Sunburst for a poster that glows upward from the bottom edge.
Raise the line count and choose silver for a finer, cooler engraving.
Turn the frame off to see the engraving on its own.
